Asbestosis is a type of interstitial lung disease caused by inhalation of asbestos fibers, which over time can lead to inflammation and scarring of lung tissue. Workers in ship-breaking are particularly at risk due to their exposure to asbestos found in older ships, where asbestos was commonly used for insulation and other materials. This chronic exposure can result in reduced lung function and various respiratory complications.

Section: Introduction
Pneumoconiosis is the general term for a class of interstitial lung disease where inhalation of dust (for example, ash dust, lead particles, pollen grains etc) has caused interstitial fibrosis.[1][2] The three most common types are asbestosis, silicosis, and black lung disease.[3] Pneumoconiosis often causes restrictive impairment,[4] although diagnosable pneumoconiosis can occur without measurable impairment of lung function.[1][2] Depending on extent and severity, it may cause death within months or years, or it may never produce symptoms. It is usually an occupational lung disease, typically from years of dust exposure during work in mining;[5] textile milling; shipbuilding, ship repairing, and/or shipbreaking; sandblasting; industrial tasks; rock drilling (subways or building pilings);[6] or agriculture.[7][8] It is one of the most common occupational diseases in the world.[9]
Section: Types
Coalworker's pneumoconiosis (CWP) / Black Lung Disease: Resulting from prolonged inhalation of coal dust, CWP leads to lung inflammation and fibrosis. Over time, this scarring impairs respiratory function, causing symptoms such as chronic cough and shortness of breath.[10] Predominantly affects coal miners, especially those engaged in underground mining operations where coal dust exposure is significant.[11] Asbestosis – asbestos: Develops from inhaling asbestos fibers, leading to lung tissue scarring and reduced lung function. Symptoms include shortness of breath, persistent cough, and chest tightness.[12] Historically prevalent among workers in shipbuilding, construction, and manufacturing, especially those handling insulation materials containing asbestos.[13] Silicosis (also known as "grinder's disease" or Potter's rot) – crystalline silica dust: Caused by inhalation of crystalline silica particles, silicosis leads to lung inflammation and scarring. Early symptoms include coughing and shortness of breath, which can progress to severe respiratory impairment.[14] Common among workers in construction, mining, and tunneling, particularly those involved in activities like stone cutting, sandblasting, and drilling, where silica dust is prevalent.[15] Bauxite fibrosis – bauxite Berylliosis – beryllium: A chronic lung disease caused by inhaling beryllium dust or fumes, leading to granuloma formation and lung scarring. Symptoms include cough, shortness of breath, fatigue, and chest pain.[16] Common in aerospace, nuclear, and manufacturing industries where beryllium is used, such as in the production of electronics and precision instruments.[17] Byssinosis – Byssinosis: (Brown Lung Disease) is caused by cotton dust inhalation and typically demonstrates a different pattern of lung abnormalities from most other pneumoconiosis. Associated with exposure to cotton, flax, or hemp dust, byssinosis causes chest tightness, coughing, and wheezing. Symptoms often worsen at the beginning of the workweek, a phenomenon known as "Monday fever".[18] Primarily affects textile workers, particularly those involved in processing raw cotton or other fibers in mills and factories.[19] Chalicosis – fine dust from stonecutting Silicosiderosis (also sometimes called iron miner's lung[20]) – mixed dust containing silica and iron[21] Labrador lung (found in miners in Labrador, Canada) – mixed dust containing iron, silica and anthophyllite, a type of asbestos Stannosis – tin oxide Baritosis - a benign type of pneumoconiosis caused by barium inhalation; it typically causes little  or no overgrowth, hardening, and/or fibrosis.[22]
Section: Diagnosis
Chest X-ray may show a characteristic patchy, subpleural, bibasilar interstitial infiltrates or small cystic radiolucencies called honeycombing, particularly in advanced disease.[27][28][29][30]

Section: Policies
The Fair Wages Resolution of 1946 required any contractor working on a public project to at least match the pay rates and other employment conditions set in the appropriate collective agreement.[88][89][90] In 1946, Purchase Tax was removed completely from kitchen fittings and crockery, while the rate was reduced on various gardening items.[82] The Employment and Training Act 1948 included provisions such as provisions as to training for employment as well as payments towards the cost of removing and resettling workers[91] The Fire Services Act 1947 introduced a new pension scheme for firefighters,[92] while the Electricity Act 1947 introduced better retirement benefits for workers in that industry.[93] The Workers' Compensation (Supplementation) Act 1948 and introduced benefits for workers with certain asbestos-related diseases which had occurred before 1948.[94] The Merchant Shipping Act 1948 and the Merchant Shipping (Safety Convention) Act 1949 were passed to improve conditions for seamen. The Shops Act 1950 consolidated previous legislation which provided that no one could be employed in a shop for more than six hours without having a break for at least 20 minutes. Section: Introduction
Pneumoconiosis is the general term for a class of interstitial lung disease where inhalation of dust (for example, ash dust, lead particles, pollen grains etc) has caused interstitial fibrosis.[1][2] The three most common types are asbestosis, silicosis, and black lung disease.[3] Pneumoconiosis often causes restrictive impairment,[4] although diagnosable pneumoconiosis can occur without measurable impairment of lung function.[1][2] Depending on extent and severity, it may cause death within months or years, or it may never produce symptoms. It is usually an occupational lung disease, typically from years of dust exposure during work in mining;[5] textile milling; shipbuilding, ship repairing, and/or shipbreaking; sandblasting; industrial tasks; rock drilling (subways or building pilings);[6] or agriculture.[7][8] It is one of the most common occupational diseases in the world.[9]
Section: Types
Coalworker's pneumoconiosis (CWP) / Black Lung Disease: Resulting from prolonged inhalation of coal dust, CWP leads to lung inflammation and fibrosis. Over time, this scarring impairs respiratory function, causing symptoms such as chronic cough and shortness of breath.[10] Predominantly affects coal miners, especially those engaged in underground mining operations where coal dust exposure is significant.[11] Asbestosis – asbestos: Develops from inhaling asbestos fibers, leading to lung tissue scarring and reduced lung function. Symptoms include shortness of breath, persistent cough, and chest tightness.[12] Historically prevalent among workers in shipbuilding, construction, and manufacturing, especially those handling insulation materials containing asbestos.[13] Silicosis (also known as "grinder's disease" or Potter's rot) – crystalline silica dust: Caused by inhalation of crystalline silica particles, silicosis leads to lung inflammation and scarring. Early symptoms include coughing and shortness of breath, which can progress to severe respiratory impairment.[14] Common among workers in construction, mining, and tunneling, particularly those involved in activities like stone cutting, sandblasting, and drilling, where silica dust is prevalent.[15] Bauxite fibrosis – bauxite Berylliosis – beryllium: A chronic lung disease caused by inhaling beryllium dust or fumes, leading to granuloma formation and lung scarring. Symptoms include cough, shortness of breath, fatigue, and chest pain.[16] Common in aerospace, nuclear, and manufacturing industries where beryllium is used, such as in the production of electronics and precision instruments.[17] Byssinosis – Byssinosis: (Brown Lung Disease) is caused by cotton dust inhalation and typically demonstrates a different pattern of lung abnormalities from most other pneumoconiosis. Associated with exposure to cotton, flax, or hemp dust, byssinosis causes chest tightness, coughing, and wheezing. Symptoms often worsen at the beginning of the workweek, a phenomenon known as "Monday fever".[18] Primarily affects textile workers, particularly those involved in processing raw cotton or other fibers in mills and factories.[19] Chalicosis – fine dust from stonecutting Silicosiderosis (also sometimes called iron miner's lung[20]) – mixed dust containing silica and iron[21] Labrador lung (found in miners in Labrador, Canada) – mixed dust containing iron, silica and anthophyllite, a type of asbestos Stannosis – tin oxide Baritosis - a benign type of pneumoconiosis caused by barium inhalation; it typically causes little  or no overgrowth, hardening, and/or fibrosis.[22]
Section: Diagnosis
Chest X-ray may show a characteristic patchy, subpleural, bibasilar interstitial infiltrates or small cystic radiolucencies called honeycombing, particularly in advanced disease.[27][28][29][30]

The Fair Wages Resolution of 1946 required any contractor working on a public project to at least match the pay rates and other employment conditions set in the appropriate collective agreement.[88][89][90] In 1946, Purchase Tax was removed completely from kitchen fittings and crockery, while the rate was reduced on various gardening items.[82] The Employment and Training Act 1948 included provisions such as provisions as to training for employment as well as payments towards the cost of removing and resettling workers[91] The Fire Services Act 1947 introduced a new pension scheme for firefighters,[92] while the Electricity Act 1947 introduced better retirement benefits for workers in that industry.[93] The Workers' Compensation (Supplementation) Act 1948 and introduced benefits for workers with certain asbestos-related diseases which had occurred before 1948.[94] The Merchant Shipping Act 1948 and the Merchant Shipping (Safety Convention) Act 1949 were passed to improve conditions for seamen. The legislation also required a lunch break of at least 45 minutes for anyone for worked between 11:30am and 2:30pm, and a half-hour tea break for anyone working between 4pm and 7pm.[95] The government also strengthened a Fair Wages Resolution, with a clause that required all employers getting government contracts to recognise the rights of their workers to join trade unions.[96] The Trades Disputes Act 1927 was repealed, and a Dock Labour Scheme was introduced in 1947 to put an end to the casual system of hiring labour in the docks.[97] This scheme gave registered dockers the legal right to minimum work and decent conditions. Through the National Dock Labour Board (on which trade unions and employers had equal representation) the unions acquired control over recruitment and dismissal. Registered dockers laid off by employers within the Scheme had the right either to be taken on by another, or to generous compensation.[98] All dockers were registered under the Dock Labour Scheme, giving them a legal right to minimum work, holidays and sick pay.[99]

Coarse particles (PM10), with diameters between 2.5 and 10 micrometers, are inhalable and can deposit in the upper airways, including the nose, throat, and bronchi.[152] Exposure to PM10 is associated with respiratory diseases (such as aggravation of asthma, bronchitis, and rhinosinusitis),[153] cardiovascular effects (such as increased risk of heart attacks and arrhythmias due to systemic inflammation).[154] Fine particles (PM2.5), with diameters less than 2.5 micrometers, can penetrate deep into the lungs, reaching the bronchioles and alveoli.[151] They are associated with chronic rhinosinusitis (PM2.5 particles can deposit in the nasal passages and sinuses, leading to inflammation and chronic rhinosinusitis),[155] respiratory diseases (exacerbation of asthma and COPD due to deep lung penetration),[156] and cardiovascular diseases from systemic inflammation and oxidative stress.[154] Ultrafine particles (PM0.1), with diameters less than 0.1 micrometers (100 nanometers), can enter the bloodstream and reach other organs, including the heart and brain.[157] Health effects include neurological effects (potential contribution to neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's due to particles crossing the blood-brain barrier),[158] cardiovascular effects such as promotion of atherosclerosis and increased risk of heart attacks.[159] PM10: Annual mean not to exceed 15 μg/m3; 24-hour mean not to exceed 45 μg/m3.[164] PM2.5: Annual mean not to exceed 5 μg/m3; 24-hour mean not to exceed 15 μg/m3.[164] Exposure above these levels increases the risk of adverse health effects.[164] Scanning electron microscopy of glass powder originated from glass bottles Scanning electron microscopy of cement Scanning electron microscopy of mortar glass powder (10%) which seems to have fibre-like structure Scanning electron microscopy of white asbestos with needle-like shape fibre Composition of particles can vary greatly depending on their sources and how they are produced. A study published in 2022 in GeoHealth concluded that eliminating energy-related fossil fuel emissions in the United States would prevent 46,900–59,400 premature deaths each year and provide $537–678 billion in benefits from avoided PM2.5-related illness and death.[216] Higher rates of infertility have been correlated with exposure to particulates.[217] Maternal PM2.5 exposure during pregnancy is also associated with high blood pressure in children.[218] Inhalation of PM2.5 – PM10 is associated with elevated risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes, such as low birth weight.[219] Exposure to PM2.5 has been associated with greater reductions in birth weight than exposure to PM10.[220] PM exposure can cause inflammation, oxidative stress, endocrine disruption, and impaired oxygen transport access to the placenta,[221] all of which are mechanisms for heightening the risk of low birth weight.[222] Overall epidemiologic and toxicological evidence suggests that a causal relationship exists between long-term exposures to PM2.5 and developmental outcomes (i.e. low birth weight).[220] Studies investigating the significance of trimester-specific exposure have proven to be inconclusive,[223] and results of international studies have been inconsistent in drawing associations of prenatal particulate matter exposure and low birth weight.[220] As perinatal outcomes have been associated with lifelong health[224][225] and exposure to particulate matter is widespread, this issue is of critical public health importance.

Section: Policies
The Fair Wages Resolution of 1946 required any contractor working on a public project to at least match the pay rates and other employment conditions set in the appropriate collective agreement.[88][89][90] In 1946, Purchase Tax was removed completely from kitchen fittings and crockery, while the rate was reduced on various gardening items.[82] The Employment and Training Act 1948 included provisions such as provisions as to training for employment as well as payments towards the cost of removing and resettling workers[91] The Fire Services Act 1947 introduced a new pension scheme for firefighters,[92] while the Electricity Act 1947 introduced better retirement benefits for workers in that industry.[93] The Workers' Compensation (Supplementation) Act 1948 and introduced benefits for workers with certain asbestos-related diseases which had occurred before 1948.[94] The Merchant Shipping Act 1948 and the Merchant Shipping (Safety Convention) Act 1949 were passed to improve conditions for seamen. The Shops Act 1950 consolidated previous legislation which provided that no one could be employed in a shop for more than six hours without having a break for at least 20 minutes. The legislation also required a lunch break of at least 45 minutes for anyone for worked between 11:30am and 2:30pm, and a half-hour tea break for anyone working between 4pm and 7pm.[95] The government also strengthened a Fair Wages Resolution, with a clause that required all employers getting government contracts to recognise the rights of their workers to join trade unions.[96] The Trades Disputes Act 1927 was repealed, and a Dock Labour Scheme was introduced in 1947 to put an end to the casual system of hiring labour in the docks.[97] This scheme gave registered dockers the legal right to minimum work and decent conditions. Through the National Dock Labour Board (on which trade unions and employers had equal representation) the unions acquired control over recruitment and dismissal. Registered dockers laid off by employers within the Scheme had the right either to be taken on by another, or to generous compensation.[98] All dockers were registered under the Dock Labour Scheme, giving them a legal right to minimum work, holidays and sick pay.[99]
